query: For titanium alloys used as structural materials, formulate one hypothesis for an intervention that could increase surface hardness and wear resistance. Specify the intervention, its proposed mechanism, the expected improvement relative to the untreated alloy, the service or test conditions under which the effect should hold, prior evidence supporting the hypothesis, and a controlled experiment with clear results that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A two‐stage, low‐temperature plasma oxy‐nitriding treatment will significantly improve the surface hardness and wear resistance of titanium alloys compared to untreated materials.
generation.material_initial_state: Titanium alloy in its standard annealed or mill-processed state (e.g., TC4 or Grade 5) with low surface hardness and limited wear resistance.
generation.intervention: Apply a two-stage, low‐temperature plasma oxy‐nitriding process: first, an oxygen-enriched plasma treatment to partially oxidize the surface and disrupt the formation of a continuous TiN layer, followed by a nitriding stage to enable rapid nitrogen diffusion.
generation.conditions: Service or test conditions simulating moderate friction and wear (e.g., pin-on-disk wear tests or similar abrasion setups) performed at temperatures where the low-temperature process maintains microstructural stability.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a composite surface layer that includes a compact, nitride-rich compound layer backed by an inter-connected porous oxygen/nitrogen diffusion zone acting as a buffer against mechanical stresses.
generation.mechanism: The initial oxygen treatment breaks up continuous TiN formation, facilitating more rapid and deeper nitrogen (and oxygen) diffusion. This results in a thicker, dual-character hardened layer that both increases the surface hardness (via solution strengthening and fine nitride dispersions) and mitigates crack propagation under wear.
generation.predicted_outcome: The treated alloy is expected to exhibit a significant increase in surface hardness and enhanced wear resistance (with a lower coefficient of friction and reduced debris formation), relative to the untreated alloy. Based on prior studies, improvements could be on the order of several tens of percent, although the exact magnitude is uncertain.
generation.baseline: Untreated titanium alloy or alloys treated by conventional single-stage nitriding processes.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effects are projected to hold under conditions where the low-temperature process avoids thermal degradation or phase transformations (e.g., β-phase formation) and in wear tests that mimic service conditions similar to those in aerospace or biomedical applications.
generation.uncertainty: While experimental evidence supports improved coating characteristics (hardness, wear resistance, and crack resistance) from modified nitriding techniques, the precise quantitative improvements and the scalability of the two-stage oxy-nitriding process remain uncertain without further comparative experiments.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of titanium alloy samples: one set undergoes the two-stage low-temperature plasma oxy-nitriding process and the other serves as a control (untreated or conventionally nitrided). Measure the surface hardness using micro-indentation tests and perform wear testing (e.g., pin-on-disk tests) to compare the coefficient of friction and wear rates between the samples.
measurements: Thickness and microstructure of the compound and diffusion layers (via SEM/TEM)
Coefficient of friction and wear rate during standardized abrasion tests
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the oxy-nitrided samples fail to show a statistically significant improvement (e.g., a predefined minimum improvement threshold in hardness and wear resistance relative to the untreated or conventionally treated samples) or if the beneficial structural features (porous buffer layer and thicker nitride compound layer) are absent, then the hypothesis is falsified.

## Abstract
To solve the problems of high nitriding temperature and long nitriding time with conventional plasma nitriding technologies, a kind of low-temperature plasma oxy-nitriding technology containing two-stage processes with different ratios of N to O was developed on a TC4 alloy in this paper. A thicker permeation coating can be obtained with this new technology compared to conventional plasma nitriding technology. The reason for this is that the oxygen introduction in the first two-hour oxy-nitriding step can break the continuous TiN layer, which facilitates the quick and deep diffusion of the solution-strengthening elements of O and N into the titanium alloy. Moreover, an inter-connected porous structure was formed under a compact compound layer, which acts as a buffer layer to absorb the external wear force. Therefore, the resultant coating showed the lowest COF values during the initial wear state, and almost no debris and cracks were detected after the wear test. For the treated samples with low hardness and no porous structure, fatigue cracks can easily form on the surface, and bulk peeling-offcan occur during the wear course.

AbstractThe study assessed the effect of ion nitriding on the properties of the surface layer of Grade 5 titanium alloy used, among others, in medicine. Titanium and its alloys have low hardness and insufficient wear resistance in conditions of friction which limits the use of these materials. The improvement of these properties is only possible by the appropriate modification of the surface layer of these alloys. The ion nitriding process was carried out in a wide temperature range, i.e., 530–590 °C, and in the time range 5–17 h. Two variants of nitriding were applied: cathodic (conventional) nitriding and nitriding using the active screen method. The research results presented in this article allow for stating that each of the applied nitriding variants improves the analysed properties (nitrogen diffusion depth, hardness, wear resistance, microstructure analysis and surface topography) of the surface layers in relation to the material before nitriding. The hardness increased in every nitriding variant (the use of the additional active screen increased the hardness to 1021 HK0.025).
